name: Pinot Noir
say: PEE-noh NWAHR, or SHPAYT-boor-goon-der in Germany

lines.s10: Pinot Noir is the pale, silky red of Burgundy: red cherry, raspberry and a quiet note of forest floor, with barely any grip.
lines.s20: Pinot Noir is the red grape of Burgundy, thin skinned, so the wine is pale and silky where most reds are dark and firm. Expect red cherry and raspberry over forest floor, with bright acidity and a long, fine finish.
lines.s45: Pinot Noir has a thin skin, and nearly everything in the glass follows from that. Its home is Burgundy, on the limestone slope of the Côte d'Or. It is pale and silky, with red cherry, raspberry and wild strawberry, bright acidity and very little grip. It is aged in French oak barrels, and with time it turns towards mushroom and forest floor. Burgundy tends to be earthier, while California and Oregon are often riper and more openly fruity. Pour it with roast duck, salmon or mushrooms. Its name is said to come from the French for pine cone, the shape of its small, tight bunches.
lines.sale: Pinot Noir is the red that goes where other reds cannot: light enough for fish, with depth enough for duck. If half the table has ordered fish and the other half meat, this is the bottle that suits you all.

glass.lead: Red cherry, raspberry and wild strawberry over rose petal and forest floor, pale and silky, with bright acidity and gentle tannin.

ladder.where: The Côte d'Or, the Willamette Valley, Germany and Tasmania
Carneros, Sonoma and California's Central Coast

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium plus to high, tannin low to medium and silky, alcohol moderate in Burgundy and medium plus from warmer sites, body light to medium.

old.where: Burgundy's Côte d'Or above all; Germany as Spätburgunder, Alsace and Sancerre
old.glass: Tends to be paler, earthier and more savoury: red cherry, raspberry and cranberry over forest floor and rose petal, with bright acidity, moderate alcohol and a firm, fine frame that asks for time.
old.cellar: Often a cold soak, then whole bunches or destemmed fruit as each estate prefers; twelve to eighteen months in French oak, more of it new for the higher tiers.

new.where: Oregon, California's cool coast, New Zealand, Tasmania, Chile and South Africa
new.glass: Typically riper and more openly fruity: black cherry, ripe raspberry and plum, often with cola and vanilla, softer acidity, a rounder body and higher alcohol. Oregon tends to sit between the two.
new.cellar: Made much as in Burgundy, though often picked riper and given a larger share of new French oak; bottled under the grape's name.

contrast.why: Burgundy is cool and marginal, so its Pinot ripens only just and keeps high acidity and modest alcohol. Sunnier New World sites give riper, darker fruit. Burgundy labels the vineyard or village; the New World names the grape.
contrast.blur: Oregon, Tasmania and the Sonoma Coast make lean, savoury wines that can pass for Burgundy, and warm recent vintages have made red Burgundy and German Spätburgunder riper and darker.
contrast.call: Forest floor, tart red cherry and moderate alcohol lean Burgundy; black cherry, cola and vanilla with softer acidity and more alcohol lean New World.

service.temp: 54 to 59 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 15 degrees Celsius: lightly cool, never warm.
service.glass: A wide Burgundy bowl, which gathers the perfume.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary. Pour a fragile old bottle gently, and decant only to leave sediment behind.
service.age: Most within five years; village and premier cru Burgundy five to fifteen, the grands crus twenty or more.

with.why: bright acidity cuts the fat, cherry fruit meets the meat
little tannin, so a red can sit with rich fish

with.dish: Wild mushrooms, or a mushroom risotto
with.why: forest floor in the wine echoes the plate
gentle tannin and ripe fruit stand up to the char

labels.means: Red Burgundy at the regional level, made from Pinot Noir; Gamay sold as Burgundy is labelled Bourgogne Gamay.
The German name, late Burgundian; Pinot Nero in Italy, Blauburgunder in Austria and the Alto Adige.
Burgundy ranks the vineyard, not the estate: grand cru is the top tier, premier cru the next.
State law asks for at least 90 per cent of the named grape, where federal law asks 75.

guest.q: Why is this red so pale? Is it a thin wine?
guest.a: Pinot Noir has thin skins, so it gives less colour and less tannin than most red grapes. Pale does not mean weak: judge it by its perfume and its length.

guest.q: Is red Burgundy a Pinot Noir?
guest.a: Almost always, yes. Burgundy labels the village or the vineyard and leaves the grape off, but the red wines of the Côte d'Or are Pinot Noir.

guest.q: Why did my red wine arrive cool?
guest.a: A light red with little tannin is fresher and more fragrant a little below room temperature. Ten minutes in an ice bucket is care, not a mistake.

compare.tell: Gamay is lighter and more candied, often with a banana or bubblegum note; Pinot Noir is silkier, with forest floor beneath the fruit.
Nebbiolo shares the pale colour but grips hard, with high tannin, tar and dried rose; Pinot Noir stays silky and gentle.
Grenache runs warmer and jammier, with strawberry jam, white pepper and higher alcohol; Pinot Noir is cooler in feel, with brighter acidity.

cards.front: Pinot Noir: where is it at home, and what gives it away?
cards.back: Burgundy's Côte d'Or. A pale, translucent ruby, silky tannin and red cherry and raspberry over forest floor: thin skins give little colour and little grip.

cards.front: Pinot Noir blind: Burgundy or the New World, what tips it?
cards.back: Tart red cherry, forest floor and moderate alcohol lean Burgundy. Black cherry, cola, vanilla, softer acidity and higher alcohol lean California; Oregon often sits between the two.

cards.front: What is Pinot Noir called in Germany, in Italy and in Austria?
cards.back: Spätburgunder in Germany, Pinot Nero in Italy, and Blauburgunder in Austria and in the Alto Adige.

questions.q: A blind red is translucent ruby, with black cherry, ripe raspberry, cola and vanilla, medium acidity, silky tannin and medium plus alcohol. The table agrees it is Pinot Noir. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: Black cherry, cola, vanilla from new oak, acidity eased to medium and medium plus alcohol point to moderate California. Gevrey-Chambertin, the Ahr and Sancerre tend to be tarter and earthier, at lower alcohol.

questions.q: A guest who loves red Burgundy asks for the same grape from Germany. Which word on the label tells you the bottle holds it?
questions.exp: Spätburgunder, late Burgundian, is the German name for Pinot Noir. Lemberger is Blaufränkisch, and Dornfelder and Trollinger are other red grapes of Germany.

questions.q: A guest finds his glass of Pinot Noir cool to the touch and asks whether the bottle was stored wrongly. What do you tell him?
opts: A light red shows more perfume served lightly cool
Every red should be poured at warm room temperature
Cooling a red takes the tannin out of it
Only an old, fragile red is ever served cool
questions.exp: Light reds with little tannin are served at 54 to 59 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 15 degrees Celsius, which lifts fruit and acidity. Cooling removes no tannin, and a warm room flattens the wine.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it and as TASTE.world, both, requires. Nothing here departs from the Codex's records on Pinot Noir; say opens on the Court's own respelling and adds the German name a guest meets on a list.

The ladder has two rungs: cool for the Côte d'Or and the Willamette Valley and moderate for Carneros, Sonoma and the Central Coast, exactly as the Court's grid reads them. Pinot Noir has no true warm home, so no warm rung is written.
The name from the pine cone is hedged in the spoken line as said to come: Bourgogne Wines states it plainly, but other reference works offer a place name instead and call the matter open.
Central Otago is left off the ladder: it is a cool continental site that gives dark, vivid fruit, and the Codex's own profile sets it apart. It stands in the New World side under New Zealand.
The Oregon floor of 90 per cent is the Codex's own reviewed fact (the Oregon reading); the Willamette Valley body is cited beside it.
Blackened redfish is the one dish from the Creole table: a low tannin red is the usual red with a meaty, charred fish.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open bourgogne-wines.com or trade.oregonwine.org directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after three fixes. The respelling, the German, Italian and Austrian names, the Oregon floor, the climate rungs and the service figures hold; the two cellar lines set a Burgundy habit on the New World side, and one label line said less than the law allows.
changed: worlds.contrast.new.cellar: Usually destemmed and often soaked cold before fermenting now reads made much as in Burgundy, though often picked riper and given a larger share of new French oak. The Codex Burgundy record makes the cold soak a Burgundian habit, so it was no New World mark.

worlds.contrast.old.cellar: Often fermented with a share of whole bunches now reads often a cold soak, then whole bunches or destemmed fruit as each estate prefers, twelve to eighteen months in French oak, more of it new for the higher tiers, as the Codex Burgundy record has it.

labels, Bourgogne Rouge: though the label seldom names the grape is struck. Regional Bourgogne labels may carry the grape and many do; the line now says Gamay sold as Burgundy is labelled Bourgogne Gamay, after the Codex Beaujolais record.
open: Whether a regional Bourgogne may print the grape on its front label: the sources read disagree, so the entry no longer says either way.
The pine cone name stays hedged as said to come, as the author left it.
